```{r}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Setup"
library(opal)
library(ggplot2)

data(io_yft_data)
data(io_yft_parameters)
data(io_yft_map)
data(io_yft_reference)

ref  <- io_yft_reference
d    <- io_yft_data
n_ts <- d$n_year

# Model outputs precomputed by data-raw/generate-io-yft-vignette-cache.R
cache <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "io_yft_vignette_cache.rds", package = "opal"))
m <- cache$models

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
options(knitr.kable.NA = "—")
fleet_name <- function(f) sprintf("%d: %s", as.integer(f), ref$fleet_names[as.integer(f)])
last <- function(df, v) df[[v]][df$ts == max(df$ts)]

series_col <- c("opal C2 (length)" = "#1E8449", "opal A (age)" = "#D35400",
                "opal A-SS3 (age)" = "#8E44AD", "SS3" = "grey20",
                "Simulated truth" = "#D4AC0D")
# A-SS3 is dashed so that A, drawn underneath, stays visible where they agree
series_lty <- setNames(rep("solid", length(series_col)), names(series_col))
series_lty[["opal A-SS3 (age)"]] <- "42"
scale_series <- list(scale_colour_manual(values = series_col, name = NULL, drop = TRUE),
                     scale_linetype_manual(values = series_lty, name = NULL, drop = TRUE))
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
            theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))
```

opal evaluates its selectivity curves on length by default and maps them to
age through the distribution of length at age. Setting the data element
`sel_basis_f` to 2 for a fishery evaluates the same curve families (logistic,
double normal, double Richards) directly on age instead. This article uses
the simulated Indian Ocean yellowfin example to show how to switch, and what
the switch does to a real-sized assessment. The data, the SS3 model and the
length-based fit C2 are described in
`vignette("io-yft-ss3-comparison", package = "opal")`.

# Why it matters here

The SS3 model of these data uses **age-based** selectivity: double normal
curves (`age_selex` pattern 20) for the fisheries, mirrors (pattern 15) for
fisheries 15 and 16, and a logistic curve (pattern 12) for the longline
index. Fit C2 uses opal's **length-based** curves, seeded from SS3's
selectivity projected onto length. Two things differ between the bases:

1. The same curve family gives a different shape of selectivity-at-age. A
   length-based curve reaches age through the spread of length at age, so it
   cannot bend as sharply as an age-based one.
2. Length-based selection also changes the predicted lengths *within* an
   age: the larger fish of an age are more likely to be caught.

Held at SS3's selectivity, opal reproduces SS3's stock size; C2 does not:

```{r}
#| label: history
h <- ref$history
knitr::kable(data.frame(h$model, B0_ratio = h$B0 / ref$ss3$ssb0, h$terminal_depletion),
             digits = c(0, 2, 3),
             col.names = c("opal fit", "B0 / SS3 B0", "Terminal SSB / B0"))
```

SS3's terminal SSB / B0 is `r fmt(last(ref$ss3$trajectory, "static_dep"), 3)`.
With age-based selectivity, opal can estimate SS3's own curves, which
separates the effect of the selectivity basis from everything else.

# Switching to age-based selectivity

## Basis and starting values

`sel_basis_f` takes one code per fishery (1 = length, 2 = age). Without it,
every fishery is length-based. Here every fishery switches:

```{r}
#| label: basis
d_age <- io_yft_data
d_age$sel_basis_f <- rep(2L, d_age$n_fishery)
```

Age-based curves take the same six `par_sel` columns as length-based ones,
centred and scaled by the ages rather than the length bins, so the
length-based starting values do not carry over. `io_yft_reference` holds
SS3's estimated `age_selex` parameters, and `convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb()`
converts patterns 20 and 12 to opal's double normal and logistic with
`basis = "age"`:

```{r}
#| label: ss3-pars
sp  <- ref$ss3$sel_par
pat <- ref$ss3$sel_pattern

# SS3 fleet whose parameters each opal fishery uses: fisheries 15 and 16
# mirror 14 (pattern 15), and the four quarterly index series 17-20 are
# SS3's survey, fleet 17.
ss3_fleet <- c(seq_len(16), rep(17L, 4))
mirror <- pat$pattern[ss3_fleet] == 15L
ss3_fleet[mirror] <- pat$special[ss3_fleet[mirror]]

ss3_pars <- t(vapply(ss3_fleet, function(fl) {
  v <- sp$value[sp$fleet == fl]
  c(v, rep(0, 6 - length(v)))
}, numeric(6)))

p_age <- io_yft_parameters
p_age$par_sel <- convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb(ss3_pars, d_age$sel_type_f,
                                           sel_lengths = d_age$len_mid,
                                           basis = "age", sel_ages = d_age$age_a)
```

```{r}
#| label: ss3-par-table
wide <- reshape(sp[sp$fleet %in% c(1:14, 17), c("fleet", "pattern", "par", "value")],
                idvar = c("fleet", "pattern"), timevar = "par", direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- c("fleet", "pattern", paste0("P", 1:6))
wide$fleet <- fleet_name(wide$fleet)
knitr::kable(wide, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "SS3's age selectivity parameters (pattern 20: peak, top, ascending and descending width, initial and final selectivity; pattern 12: inflection and width).")
```

SS3's final selectivity is −999 for every double normal: "no adjustment",
so the descending limb is the plain normal curve. `convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb()`
converts −999 to −9, which forces selectivity at the oldest age close to
zero and, through the rescaling of the descending limb, pulls the whole limb
down: by up to 0.6 for fishery 11 here. Both SS3 and opal rescale the limb
so that it ends at the final selectivity, so setting the final selectivity
to the unadjusted curve's own value at the oldest age leaves the limb
unchanged, which reproduces "no adjustment" exactly:

```{r}
#| label: no-adjustment
# Unadjusted descending limb at the oldest age, as in sel_double_normal()
dn_unadjusted_end <- function(par, x) {
  n <- length(x)
  bin_width <- x[2] - x[1]
  peak <- mean(x) + par[1] * sd(x)
  peak2 <- peak + bin_width + (0.99 * x[n] - peak - bin_width) / (1 + exp(-par[2]))
  exp(-(x[n] - peak2)^2 / (exp(par[4]) * sd(x)^2))
}
for (f in which(d_age$sel_type_f == 2L & ss3_pars[, 6] <= -999)) {
  p_age$par_sel[f, 6] <- max(qlogis(dn_unadjusted_end(p_age$par_sel[f, ], d_age$age_a)), -20)
}
```

The final selectivity stays fixed when the other parameters are estimated,
so this is exact at the starting values and an approximation once the peak
or descending width move away from them.

## Bounds

opal bounds estimated selectivity parameters to ±7, which suits curves
centred and scaled on the length bins. On the age scale, SS3's plateau and
ascending-width parameters for several fisheries are near −10 to −15
(SS3 bounds them at ±20). `get_bounds()` needs only the names of the
estimated parameters, so the default bounds can be taken and widened for
`par_sel`:

```{r}
#| label: bounds
age_bounds <- function(parameters, map, lim = 20) {
  active <- unlist(lapply(names(parameters), function(n)
    rep(n, if (is.null(map[[n]])) length(parameters[[n]]) else nlevels(droplevels(map[[n]])))))
  b <- get_bounds(list(par = setNames(numeric(length(active)), active)), parameters)
  b$lower[b$parameter == "par_sel"] <- -lim
  b$upper[b$parameter == "par_sel"] <- lim
  b
}
```

## Check 1: the converted curves reproduce SS3's

The age-based curves do not use the age–length key, so they can be computed
directly with `get_selectivity()`:

```{r}
#| label: sel-start
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Selectivity-at-age: SS3's, and opal's age-based curves at the converted SS3 parameters."
sel0 <- get_selectivity(d_age, p_age$par_sel, pla = NULL, len_mid = d_age$len_mid,
                        age_a = d_age$age_a)[, 1, ]
s0 <- data.frame(fishery = rep(seq_len(nrow(sel0)), times = ncol(sel0)),
                 age = rep(d_age$age_a, each = nrow(sel0)), sel = as.vector(sel0))
cmp <- merge(s0, ref$ss3$sel_age, by = c("fishery", "age"), suffixes = c("_opal", "_ss3"))
ggplot(cmp[cmp$fishery <= 17, ], aes(age)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sel_ss3, colour = "SS3"), linewidth = 2, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = sel_opal, colour = "opal A (age)"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ fishery, ncol = 4, labeller = as_labeller(fleet_name)) +
  scale_series +
  labs(x = "Age (quarters)", y = "Selectivity")
```

The largest difference over all fisheries and ages is
`r fmt(max(abs(cmp$sel_opal - cmp$sel_ss3)), 4)`.

## Check 2: stock size at SS3's parameters

With these curves and every other parameter at SS3's solution, opal's stock
trajectory should be the one it gives with SS3's selectivity-at-age supplied
directly as a fixed matrix (`sel_fa_external`). Neither run is fitted:

```{r}
#| label: bridge
#| eval: false
start <- opal_obj(d_age, p_age, io_yft_map, bounds = age_bounds(p_age, io_yft_map))

d_ext <- d_age
sa <- ref$ss3$sel_age
d_ext$sel_fa_external <- matrix(0, d_ext$n_fishery, d_ext$n_age)
d_ext$sel_fa_external[cbind(sa$fishery, match(sa$age, d_ext$age_a))] <- sa$sel
start_ext <- opal_obj(d_ext, p_age, io_yft_map, bounds = age_bounds(p_age, io_yft_map))

ssb_age <- opal_report(start)$spawning_biomass_y
ssb_ext <- opal_report(start_ext)$spawning_biomass_y
```

```{r}
#| label: bridge-result
pct <- function(a, b) 100 * abs(a$ssb / b$ssb - 1)
ss3_traj <- ref$ss3$trajectory
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  comparison = c("Age-based curves vs SS3's fixed matrix",
                 "Age-based curves vs SS3", "SS3's fixed matrix vs SS3"),
  mean = c(mean(pct(m$A_start$trajectory, m$E_start$trajectory)),
           mean(pct(m$A_start$trajectory, ss3_traj)), mean(pct(m$E_start$trajectory, ss3_traj))),
  max = c(max(pct(m$A_start$trajectory, m$E_start$trajectory)),
          max(pct(m$A_start$trajectory, ss3_traj)), max(pct(m$E_start$trajectory, ss3_traj)))),
  digits = 3, col.names = c("Spawning biomass at SS3's parameters", "Mean |% diff|", "Max |% diff|"))
```

The two opal runs agree to within
`r fmt(max(pct(m$A_start$trajectory, m$E_start$trajectory)), 3)`%. Both
differ from SS3 by up to 10%, which comes from when catch is removed within
the quarter, not from selectivity (see the comparison article).

# Fits

## What is estimated

Two age-based fits are compared with C2:

* **A** uses C2's map exactly: `log_B0`, the recruitment deviations, the
  four catchabilities and the same 49 selectivity parameters. The basis is
  the only difference from C2.
* **A-SS3** estimates every selectivity parameter SS3 estimated (phase > 0):
  P1–P4 of each double normal and both logistic parameters, with SS3's
  mirrors. That adds the nine parameters C2 fixes because the length data do
  not inform them under length-based selectivity.

```{r}
#| label: map-ss3
est <- matrix(NA_integer_, d_age$n_fishery, 6)
k <- 0L
for (fl in unique(ss3_fleet)) {
  cols <- sp$par[sp$fleet == fl & sp$phase > 0]
  ids <- k + seq_along(cols)
  k <- k + length(cols)
  for (f in which(ss3_fleet == fl)) est[f, cols] <- ids
}
map_ss3 <- io_yft_map
map_ss3$par_sel <- factor(as.vector(est))

c(C2_and_A = nlevels(io_yft_map$par_sel), A_SS3 = nlevels(map_ss3$par_sel))
```

Each fit takes a few minutes, so the article reads stored results. The fits
were made from exactly these inputs; `data-raw/generate-io-yft-age-fits.R`
adds Newton steps and `opal_check()`, as for C2.

```{r}
#| label: fit
#| eval: false
fit_a     <- opal_fit(opal_obj(d_age, p_age, io_yft_map,
                               bounds = age_bounds(p_age, io_yft_map)), n_passes = 2L)
fit_a_ss3 <- opal_fit(opal_obj(d_age, p_age, map_ss3,
                               bounds = age_bounds(p_age, map_ss3)), n_passes = 2L)

# The stored fits
fit_a     <- opal_read(system.file("extdata", "io_yft_age_fit.rds", package = "opal"))
fit_a_ss3 <- opal_read(system.file("extdata", "io_yft_age_ss3_fit.rds", package = "opal"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fit-table
fits <- list("opal C2 (length)" = m$C2, "opal A (age)" = m$A, "opal A-SS3 (age)" = m$A_ss3)
fit_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm) {
  x <- fits[[nm]]
  data.frame(model = nm, sel = x$sel_free, n_par = x$fit$n_par,
             objective = x$objective, t(x$nll),
             grad = formatC(x$fit$max_gradient, format = "e", digits = 1),
             check = if (isTRUE(x$fit$passes)) "passed" else "failed")
}))
knitr::kable(fit_tab[, c("model", "sel", "n_par", "objective", "index", "length",
                         "recruitment", "prior", "grad", "check")],
             digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Model", "Selectivity parameters", "Estimated parameters",
                           "Objective", "Index", "Length comps", "Recruitment",
                           "Priors", "Max |gradient|", "opal_check()"))
```

All three fits converge and pass `opal_check()`. The objectives are not
comparable across the two bases, because of the priors. opal puts an N(0, 2)
prior on every element of `par_sel`, fixed or estimated. The parameters are
centred and scaled by the length bins for C2 and by the ages for A, so the
same prior is a different prior on the curves. SS3's plateau and
ascending-width parameters are near −10 to −15 on the age scale, so A's
prior term is `r fmt(m$A$nll[["prior"]] - m$C2$nll[["prior"]], 0)` larger
than C2's: the whole of the difference in objective and more.

The data terms compare directly. C2 and A fit the index equally well, and A
fits the length compositions better, by
`r fmt(m$C2$nll[["length"]] - m$A$nll[["length"]], 1)` likelihood units with
the same number of parameters. Estimating the nine extra parameters (A-SS3)
improves the length compositions by only
`r fmt(m$A$nll[["length"]] - m$A_ss3$nll[["length"]], 2)`; the lower
objective of A-SS3 comes from the prior, as those parameters move towards
its mean. As under length-based selectivity, the data do not inform them.

# Selectivity

```{r}
#| label: sel-fitted
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Selectivity-at-age: SS3's, C2's length-based curves mapped to age, and the age-based fits."
sa <- rbind(
  data.frame(ref$ss3$sel_age, series = "SS3"),
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm)
    data.frame(fits[[nm]]$sel_age, series = nm))))
sa$series <- factor(sa$series, names(series_col))
ggplot(sa[sa$fishery <= 17, ], aes(age, sel, colour = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ fishery, ncol = 4, labeller = as_labeller(fleet_name)) +
  scale_series +
  labs(x = "Age (quarters)", y = "Selectivity")
```

Fisheries 15 and 16 mirror 14, and panel 17 stands for all four quarterly
index series.

The age-based fits follow SS3's ascending limbs closely, including the sharp
rises that C2's length-based curves smooth out. Where they depart from SS3,
C2 departs in the same direction: fishery 5's ascending limb is much
shallower than SS3's, and fisheries 6, 8 and 11 keep selectivity higher
than SS3 at intermediate ages. A and A-SS3 differ only for fishery 9. A
holds its descending width at SS3's value while its peak moves, so its
selectivity drops to zero within two quarters; A-SS3 estimates the width
and gives a gradual decline. The length compositions barely distinguish the
two (0.04 likelihood units in total).

# Fits to the data

## Length compositions

```{r}
#| label: comp-aggregate
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Length compositions aggregated over all observations for each fishery, weighted by sample size: observed (bars) and each model's predictions."
obs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(d$lf_fishery_f), function(j) {
  o <- d$lf_obs_data$obs[[j]]
  o <- o / rowSums(o)
  n <- d$lf_n_fi[[j]]
  data.frame(fishery = d$lf_fishery_f[j], bin = d$len_lower, observed = colSums(o * n) / sum(n))
}))
lines <- rbind(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm)
    data.frame(fishery = fits[[nm]]$lf$fishery, bin = fits[[nm]]$lf$bin,
               value = fits[[nm]]$lf$predicted, series = nm))),
  data.frame(fishery = ref$ss3$lf$fishery, bin = ref$ss3$lf$bin,
             value = ref$ss3$lf$expected, series = "SS3"))
lines$series <- factor(lines$series, names(series_col))
width <- diff(d$len_lower[1:2])
ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = obs, aes(bin + width / 2, observed), fill = "grey80", width = width) +
  geom_line(data = lines, aes(bin + width / 2, value, colour = series, linetype = series),
            linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ fishery, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y", labeller = as_labeller(fleet_name)) +
  scale_series +
  labs(x = "Length (cm)", y = "Proportion")
```

## Index

```{r}
#| label: index-rmse
rmse <- function(o, p) sqrt(mean((log(o) - log(p))^2))
cp <- d$cpue_data
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = c(names(fits), "SS3"),
  rmse = c(vapply(fits, function(x) rmse(cp$value, x$cpue$pred), numeric(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE),
           rmse(ref$ss3$cpue$obs, ref$ss3$cpue$expected))),
  digits = 4, col.names = c("Model", "RMSE of log index residuals"))
```

# Stock status

```{r}
#| label: trajectories
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Spawning biomass (top) and static depletion SSB / B0 (bottom) of each fit, SS3 and the simulated truth."
traj <- rbind(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm) data.frame(fits[[nm]]$trajectory, series = nm))),
  data.frame(ref$ss3$trajectory, series = "SS3"),
  data.frame(ref$truth$trajectory, series = "Simulated truth"))
traj$series <- factor(traj$series, names(series_col))
long <- rbind(data.frame(ts = traj$ts, series = traj$series, value = traj$ssb / 1e6,
                         panel = "Spawning biomass (million t)"),
              data.frame(ts = traj$ts, series = traj$series, value = traj$static_dep,
                         panel = "SSB / B0"))
ggplot(long, aes(ts, value, colour = series, linetype = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_series +
  labs(x = "Time step (quarter)", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: status-table
status <- data.frame(
  model = c(names(fits), "SS3", "Simulated truth"),
  B0 = c(vapply(fits, `[[`, numeric(1), "B0", USE.NAMES = FALSE), ref$ss3$ssb0, ref$truth$b0),
  dep = c(vapply(fits, function(x) last(x$trajectory, "static_dep"), numeric(1),
                 USE.NAMES = FALSE),
          last(ref$ss3$trajectory, "static_dep"), last(ref$truth$trajectory, "static_dep")))
status$B0_ss3 <- status$B0 / ref$ss3$ssb0
status$B0_truth <- status$B0 / ref$truth$b0
knitr::kable(status[, c("model", "B0_ss3", "B0_truth", "dep")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Model", "B0 / SS3 B0", "B0 / true B0", "Terminal SSB / B0"))
```

# Summary

* Switching a fishery to age-based selectivity takes one data element,
  `sel_basis_f = 2`, and starting values on the age scale, which
  `convert_ss3_selex_to_rtmb(basis = "age")` provides from SS3's patterns 20
  and 12. SS3's −999 "no adjustment" final selectivity needs the extra step
  shown above, and SS3's values need wider `par_sel` bounds than opal's
  default.
* At SS3's parameters, the converted curves reproduce SS3's
  selectivity-at-age, and the stock trajectory is the one opal gives with
  SS3's selectivity supplied as a fixed matrix.
* Estimated with C2's map, the age-based fit A fits the length compositions
  better than the length-based C2, with B0
  `r fmt(m$A$B0 / ref$ss3$ssb0, 2)` × SS3's and terminal depletion
  `r fmt(last(m$A$trajectory, "static_dep"), 3)`, against
  `r fmt(m$C2$B0 / ref$ss3$ssb0, 2)` × and
  `r fmt(last(m$C2$trajectory, "static_dep"), 3)` for C2 and
  `r fmt(last(ref$ss3$trajectory, "static_dep"), 3)` for SS3. Estimating
  every parameter SS3 estimated (A-SS3) changes neither.
* So the selectivity basis does not explain why opal's estimated stock is
  smaller than SS3's: with SS3's curve families on SS3's basis, estimated
  from the same data, opal moves no closer to SS3. Held at SS3's estimates, the same curves
  give B0 `r fmt(h$B0[2] / ref$ss3$ssb0, 2)` × SS3's. The remaining
  differences are in the rest of the model (catch timing within the quarter,
  the index and the priors; see the comparison article).
* The N(0, 2) selectivity prior is a stronger constraint on the age scale
  than on the length scale here. It is part of what differs between A and
  SS3, which has no prior on selectivity.

The outputs in this article were computed with opal `r cache$opal`
(commit `r cache$commit`) by `data-raw/generate-io-yft-vignette-cache.R`.
